opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly I think the answer has shifted over the past few years. If you'd asked me five or six years ago, I might have said, "Well, if a quadruped can walk robustly over rough terrain, stairs, slopes, without falling, then we're basically there." And to some extent we've achieved that. With reinforcement learning in simulation and sim-to-real transfer, we can now train policies that handle really challenging terrain, sometimes better than classical model-based controllers.

But I don't think that means locomotion is solved. For me, the bar is closer to what animals and humans can do. Think about a dog running through a forest. It's not just placing its feet stably. It's jumping over logs, squeezing under branches, recovering when it slips on mud, adapting instantly when the ground behaves unexpectedly, and doing all of that while paying attention to something else entirely. Locomotion is almost an afterthought for the animal. It just works, everywhere, all the time.

So for me, solved would mean a few things. First, reliability: not 95% or 99%, but walking for hours or days in completely unstructured environments without anyone stepping in. Second, generality: the same controller, or the same learning approach, working across very different environments, from snow to rubble to a crowded building, without retuning for each one. Third, agility: running, jumping, climbing, parkour-style motions, the full dynamic range of the hardware, not just careful, conservative walking. And fourth, and this is the one I find most interesting, integration with perception and higher-level tasks. Locomotion shouldn't be an isolated skill. The robot should move through the world in service of doing something, whether that's carrying an object, opening a door, or inspecting a site, and moving the body and interacting with the world should blend together.

We're making really fast progress on all of these, but especially for perception, robustness in truly unseen conditions, and loco-manipulation, there's still a real gap. So I'd say the basic problem of walking is in good shape. Locomotion at the level of an animal, that you can just trust out in the world, is still open, and that's what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes animal-like locomotion and operation across varied environments, but does not clearly state that a robot must be able to go anywhere a human can go.

r002.rationale: It calls for walking for hours or days in unstructured environments without intervention and being trustworthy in the world, conveying reliability people can take for granted.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think it's a harder one to answer than it sounds, because the goalposts keep moving.

If you had asked me a few years ago, I would have said something like: a legged robot that can walk over rough terrain outdoors without falling. And we're basically there. We've seen quadrupeds doing hikes in the Alps, going through forests, handling stairs, gravel, snow. Learning-based controllers trained in simulation made that almost routine. So by that old definition, locomotion is in some sense solved.

But that's not how I'd frame it today. For me the bar is: can a robot go anywhere a human or an animal of comparable size can go, and do it reliably enough that you stop thinking about the legs at all. The locomotion becomes a background capability, like it is for us. You don't consciously think about walking when you cross a room, you just think about the task.

And when you put it that way, there's still a lot missing. One piece is perception integrated deeply into the control. Most of the impressive results are still fairly reactive, feeling the terrain through contact and adjusting. Truly anticipatory behavior, where the robot looks ahead, decides to step on this rock and not that one, maybe jumps, maybe climbs, that's much less mature. Another piece is robustness over long horizons. A demo that works for ten minutes is very different from a system that works for a year with no one in the loop. And then there's the whole category of things that blur the line between locomotion and manipulation. Opening a door while balancing, pushing through brush, using your hands to climb. Humans do that constantly, and for robots it's still very early.

So my honest answer is that I'd consider it solved when it stops being a research topic and becomes an engineering problem. When new terrain, new robot, new task doesn't mean a new paper, it just means a bit of tuning and data. We're moving in that direction quickly, especially with simulation and sim-to-real getting so good, but I don't think we're there yet.

r001.rationale: The response says locomotion is solved when a robot can go anywhere a human or comparable-sized animal can go.

r002.rationale: It requires reliable locomotion that becomes a background capability people no longer have to think about.

astra-6.text:
I think I would consider it solved when you can give a robot a destination and trust it to get there without having to think about how it moves. It should handle different terrain, unexpected obstacles, and disturbances, and if it falls, it should be able to get back up and continue.

But it also needs to understand its limits. If a gap is too wide or a slope is too steep, it should recognize that and find another way, rather than just try and fail. So it’s not necessarily about being able to go everywhere. It’s about being reliable enough that locomotion becomes something you can take for granted and build other capabilities on top of.

r001.rationale: The response says locomotion need not let a robot go everywhere; it does not say robots must be able to go anywhere a human can.

r002.rationale: It says locomotion should be reliable enough to take for granted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by solved. You can have a robot walking very nicely in a lab, but that doesn’t mean you can put it somewhere you’ve never tested and expect it to work. For me, the goal would be to take a robot out into the world and not have to think about its locomotion. You give it a task, and you can trust it to get there, whether there are stairs, slippery ground, or obstacles along the way.

And that doesn’t necessarily mean it never falls. We fall too. But it should recognize when it’s getting into trouble, recover when it can, and get back up if it does fall. Once moving around is something we can take for granted, and we can focus on what the robot is actually supposed to do, then I’d be comfortable calling locomotion solved.

r001.rationale: The response describes reliable movement in unfamiliar real-world settings and gives examples, but it does not state that the robot must go anywhere a human can go.

r002.rationale: It says people should be able to take the robot’s movement for granted and trust it to reach its task destination.
